strengths: Significant and well-motivated dataset contribution: HydraFake-100K systematically covers classic, public, and newly reproduced advanced deepfake methods (relighting, restoration, personalization, generative swapping, VAR architectures), and the hierarchical evaluation protocol (in-domain / cross-model / cross-forgery / cross-domain) is a meaningful advance over the standard FF++-train/test-others protocol.

The paper is comprehensive and technically solid: a full training pipeline (pattern-guided SFT, MiPO preference alignment, P-GRPO with pattern-aware rewards) is clearly specified, with LoRA configurations, hyperparameters, annotation pipelines, and prompt templates included, supporting reproducibility.

Strong empirical evidence: 10 fine-tuned SOTA detectors, 6 open-source MLLMs, and 2 closed-source MLLMs are compared; VERITAS achieves a clear +6.0% averaged gain, and the qualitative analysis that MLLM-based detectors excel at high-resolution but fail on low-resolution images is an interesting and honest finding.

Thorough ablation studies cover the value of pattern-aware reasoning vs. post-hoc explanation and flexible CoT, individual reward components in P-GRPO, training-stage ordering (MiPO before P-GRPO), cold-start necessity, base model choice, and robustness to JPEG/blur perturbations.
Evaluation goes beyond accuracy to include reasoning quality (score + ELO judging), precision/recall per subset, and an ethics statement addressing the sensitive nature of facial data.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: 'pattern-aware reasoning' borrows heavily from existing work (s1, planning/reflection patterns), MiPO is essentially a DPO variant with mixed non-preference data, and P-GRPO is GRPO with a modified reward table; the core contribution is an application of known post-training recipes to a new domain rather than new learning techniques.

Possible shortcut-learning and benchmark-easiness concerns: VERITAS reaches 99.8-99.9% on several cross-model splits, which the paper itself partially attributes to high-resolution advantages; performance collapses on low-resolution subsets (e.g., 58.6% on DeepFaceLab, 90.9% on FF++ vs. 100% on high-res), suggesting the model exploits resolution/quality cues as much as forensic reasoning, and the 'generalizable detection' claim should be tempered.

The near-saturated results raise dataset validity questions: potential leakage of test sources (FFHQ, FF++, CelebA, public scraped data) into the InternVL3-8B pretraining distribution is not analyzed, which is a common confound for MLLM-based detectors evaluated on public imagery.

Claims of 'faithful' and 'transparent' reasoning are not rigorously verified: reasoning quality is judged by GPT-4o/Gemini-2.5-Pro, which are known to favor verbose, structured outputs of the style VERITAS was explicitly trained to produce, creating a self-confirmation bias; no human faithfulness study of reasoning-to-answer correspondence is provided.

Annotation reliance on MLLM ensembles (Qwen2.5-VL-72B, Kimi-VL, InternVL3-78B, Qwen3-235B) with limited human verification (only ~3K preference pairs manually checked) means SFT reasoning traces may contain factual hallucinations that are then reinforced.

Some baselines lack detail: 'Flexible Reasoning' and 'Post-hoc Explanation' ablation baselines are underspecified, and a dedicated deepfake-detection baseline trained with the same LoRA budget on the same data would strengthen attribution of gains to the reasoning pipeline vs. simply fine-tuning a strong base model.
The 'Project Page' link is empty in the manuscript, and although data release is promised, reproducibility of the dataset itself (reimplementation of 10 advanced generators) is not yet verifiable.

strengths: The HydraFake dataset is a substantial and timely contribution: it aggregates real images from 8 sources across resolutions and fakes from classic, public, and self-constructed advanced forgery types, with a hierarchical (in-domain / cross-model / cross-forgery / cross-domain) evaluation protocol that more closely reflects practical deployment than the standard FF++ train/test regime.

The empirical study is broad: 10 specialized detectors plus 4 open-source and 2 closed-source MLLMs are evaluated, and the finding that existing detectors generalize cross-model but fail cross-forgery/cross-domain is a useful and well-supported diagnostic for the community.

VERITAS achieves clear state-of-the-art results (90.7 avg. accuracy vs. 82.2 for the best prior detector), with a 32.4% gain over its base MLLM, and the appendix provides detailed per-subset accuracy/precision/recall breakdowns.

Ablations are fairly thorough: reasoning paradigms (Table 2), training stages (Figure 5), reward components (Table 3), base models and scales (Table 4), robustness to compression/blur (Table 6), and reasoning-quality scoring/ELO (Table 5).
The full annotation pipeline, prompt templates, and ethics statement are provided, supporting reproducibility of the data construction and training recipe.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited. The core recipe (SFT cold-start with structured CoT tags, preference optimization, then GRPO-style RL with format/answer rewards) closely follows established post-training practice (e.g., DeepSeek-R1-style pipelines); 'pattern-aware reasoning' reduces to five heuristic output tags, and MiPO is a modest variant of DPO with mixed rejected samples. The paper does not provide a compelling analysis of why these specific patterns, rather than generic long CoT, drive the gains beyond the single ablation in Table 2.

Serious benchmark-integrity concerns undermine some headline claims. Several evaluation subsets are self-constructed by the authors, and the SFT annotation pipeline (Stage-2 prompt, Figure 15) explicitly conditions on the ground truth ('the given image is a fake generated by {Forgery Type}') and the forgery type. Training the model on reasoning traces derived from known answers and known generator identities risks teaching shortcuts that inflate scores on self-constructed splits. The suspiciously near-ceiling results (e.g., 99.8–99.9 on HART/Infinity/StarryAI, 100.0 on FFHQ-based in-domain subsets) are consistent with such shortcut learning or overly easy subsets (e.g., WILD/TalkingHeadBench subsets generated with 'template-like' prompts), and the paper does not control for this.

The claim of 'transparent and faithful' reasoning is weakly supported. Faithfulness is evaluated only via MLLM-as-judge scoring and ELO (GPT-4o / Gemini-2.5-Pro judges, which are also baselines), with no human evaluation of faithfulness or counterfactual/consistency tests. The qualitative examples in the appendix contain generic, repetitive forensic language ('medium-hard to detect'), and the Stage-3 rewriting is performed without access to the image, inviting hallucinated evidence.

The reflection-quality reward relies on UnifiedReward-Qwen-3B, a general-purpose reward model with no demonstrated forensic competence; no validation of this reward's reliability on deepfake reflections is provided.

Reproducibility and statistical rigor are limited: single base model with LoRA, no seeds/variance reporting, and accuracy as the primary metric (precision/recall relegated to the appendix), even though class balance and failure modes (e.g., near-zero recall of zero-shot MLLMs) are central to the story.

Data legality and curation details are thin for crawled social-media content (watermarks cropped out of Xiaohongshu/TikTok images), which raises copyright and consent concerns that the brief ethics statement does not fully address.

Several presentation issues: undefined/inconsistent notation in Eq. (2), missing hyperlink content ('Project Page:' is empty), and imprecise claims (e.g., 'first attempt to introduce human-like reasoning into deepfake detection' overlooks closely related concurrent work cited by the authors themselves, such as Gao et al. 2025 and Xia et al. 2025).

strengths: HydraFake is a well-motivated and comprehensive benchmark (100K images, 21+ forgery sources, four-level hierarchical evaluation) that directly addresses a real gap between academic deepfake evaluation and practical deployment scenarios; the finding that existing detectors generalize well cross-model but poorly cross-forgery/cross-domain is a valuable empirical contribution to the community.

Substantial and convincing empirical results: VERITAS achieves a 6.0% average gain over the best prior detector (90.7% vs. 84.7%) and +32.4% over its base MLLM, with detailed per-subset accuracy/precision/recall tables and comparisons against 10 specialized detectors, 4 open MLLMs, and GPT-4o/Gemini-2.5-Pro.

Thorough ablation studies covering the reasoning paradigm (Table 2), training stages (Figure 5), cold-start settings (Figure 6), reward components (Table 3), and base model choices/scales (Table 4), plus robustness testing under JPEG compression and blur (Table 6), which together support the design choices.
The paper clearly articulates the distinction between post-hoc explanation and reasoning-based detection (Appendix A.2) and positions the work carefully against prior MLLM-based deepfake detectors.

Ethics statement is present; the dataset construction (quality control, manual filtering, identity splits) and full annotation prompts are documented in the appendix, aiding reproducibility of the methodology.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: the overall recipe (SFT cold-start + preference optimization + GRPO-style RL with pattern/format rewards) closely follows the now-standard DeepSeek-R1-style post-training pipeline, and the five 'thinking patterns' are heuristic; the motivation for pattern-aware over flexible reasoning rests largely on empirical gains rather than deeper analysis.

The claimed 'transparent and faithful' reasoning is evaluated mainly via LLM-as-judge (GPT-4o / Gemini-2.5-Pro scoring and ELO), which is a weak and potentially circular proxy; the SFT reasoning traces are largely synthesized by Qwen3-235B rewriting MLLM explanations, raising concerns about whether the reasoning genuinely reflects the model's decision process or is post-hoc rationalization. No human faithfulness evaluation (e.g., human study) is reported.

Some evidence suggests possible shortcuts or uneven difficulty: near-perfect 99.9% on cross-model splits (vs. 93-94% for prior detectors) is a suspiciously large jump, while performance on low-resolution/degraded subsets remains poor (e.g., 58.6% on DeepFaceLab, below Gemini-2.5-Pro's 67.2%), and the reflection-quality reward relies on a small reward model (UnifiedReward-Qwen-3B) whose reliability for this novel criterion is not validated.

No variance/significance reporting across runs, and several baselines may be under-tuned relative to their original settings; the fairness of comparing fine-tuned VERITAS against zero-shot closed-source MLLMs and against specialized detectors trained with the authors' protocol could be discussed more rigorously.

Reproducibility resources appear incomplete: the 'Project Page' is empty in the manuscript, and release details (exact data licensing for crawled social-media images, image-level splits, code) are not fully specified; MiPO is also close to existing DPO variants and its precise difference from standard mixed-preference methods could be sharpened.

strengths: Substantial dataset contribution: HydraFake provides ~100K images spanning classic, public, and self-constructed advanced deepfakes (including relighting, restoration, personalization, VAR-based generation, and in-the-wild social media fakes), with a hierarchical 4-level OOD evaluation protocol that is more realistic than the standard FF++-based protocol.

Comprehensive and convincing experimental design: comparisons against 10 fine-tuned vision detectors, 6 generic MLLMs, and 5 MLLM-based forgery detectors; results are broken down per subset with accuracy, precision, and recall, including cross-benchmark evaluation (AIGIBench, LOKI, FakeClue, etc.), robustness to JPEG/blur perturbations, and efficiency analysis.

Thorough ablation studies: the paper dissects the effect of each reasoning pattern (Table 5), each training stage (Figure 4), each reward component (Table 3), MiPO non-preference types (Table 6), base models/model sizes, hyperparameters, training data selection for P-GRPO, and reward models—giving strong support for design choices.

The two-stage pipeline (pattern-guided cold-start with MiPO, then pattern-aware GRPO) is well-motivated, and the empirical claim that cold-start is necessary for artifact-heavy tasks (unlike semantic-rich AIGC tasks) is an interesting, well-supported observation.

Large, detailed appendix covering data construction, annotation pipelines, prompt templates, failure analysis, ethics, and limitations, which supports reproducibility and transparency of the reasoning outputs.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is incremental: 'pattern-aware reasoning' is essentially structured CoT with fixed XML tags (<fast>, <planning>, <reasoning>, <reflection>, <conclusion>), and MiPO/P-GRPO are relatively direct adaptations of existing DPO-style and GRPO-style objectives with hand-crafted reward shaping (Eq. 5). The reward design (e.g., -1.0 penalty for incorrect reflection, +2.0 for correct answers with any pattern) is heuristic and not deeply analyzed for its effect on the learned behavior.

The headline evaluation is primarily on the authors' own HydraFake benchmark, whose training/test splits, subset composition, and difficulty calibration are defined by the same authors; while VERITAS-MINI and cross-benchmark results (Table 14-15) partially mitigate this, there is an inherent advantage to the method trained and tuned within the same data ecosystem.

Claims of 'transparent and faithful' reasoning are supported mainly by qualitative examples and MLLM-as-a-judge evaluations (GPT-4o/Gemini judge also used as baselines, and the paper itself shows judge models can't detect these fakes), rather than human expert evaluation of factual grounding of the reasoning traces; hallucinated forensic reasoning risk is not quantitatively measured.

The reflection-quality reward relies on an external reward model (UnifiedReward-Qwen-3B), introducing a potential feedback loop / reward-hacking channel that is only superficially analyzed; novelty of 'reflection' is also a fairly subjective criterion.

Notable performance weaknesses are acknowledged but not fully resolved: low-resolution cross-domain subsets (DeepFaceLab 58.6, FFIW) remain near random-to-moderate, and face relighting (IC-Light, 75.7) is actually worse than the baseline Effort (94.8), indicating the approach is strongly resolution/quality dependent—limiting the claimed generality in practical 'in-the-wild' settings.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in the submitted version: the 'Project Page:' placeholder is empty, and dataset/statistics release plans are not clearly stated; also, crawled social media data (Xiaohongshu/TikTok, watermark cropping) raises additional consent/provenance questions only partially addressed in the ethics statement.

strengths: The HydraFake benchmark is a substantial and well-motivated resource: it aggregates classic, public, and self-constructed deepfake data (100K images) with a hierarchical evaluation protocol (in-domain, cross-model, cross-forgery, cross-domain) that better reflects practical deployment than the standard FF++-train/testing regime.

The empirical study is broad and mostly convincing: 10 fine-tuned SOTA detectors, 4 open-source and 2 closed-source MLLMs, and 5 MLLM-based forgery detectors are compared under a unified protocol, revealing a real and previously under-quantified gap (cross-model is nearly solved at ~90%+ while cross-forgery/cross-domain drop sharply).

Ablations are unusually thorough: effect of each reasoning pattern, each training stage, reward components, base model choice, hyperparameters (G, KL strength), reward model choice, efficiency, robustness to compression/blur, and cross-benchmark evaluation on LOKI/AIGIBench/FakeClue/Forensics-Bench.

The two-stage pipeline is well-executed engineering: cold-start SFT plus MiPO before P-GRPO is shown empirically to matter (Figure 4/5), and the finding that pure RL underperforms without cold-start is a useful negative result for the community.
The paper is transparent about limitations (low-resolution weakness, image-only scope) and includes failure analysis, ethics statement, and detailed prompt templates.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. The core contributions are largely combinations of known components: template-tagged CoT ('<fast>', '<planning>', '<reflection>' are prompt scaffolds), a DPO-style preference loss (MiPO), and GRPO with a hand-crafted, ad-hoc reward table (Eq. 5 with magic values 2.0/1.0/-0.5/-1.0). The 'pattern-aware' framing is not clearly more than prompt engineering, and the motivating 'human forensic process' analogy is asserted rather than established (no evidence the tags correspond to genuine cognitive stages).

The central claim of 'faithful' and 'transparent' reasoning is weakly validated. SFT reasoning traces are generated by MLLMs (Qwen2.5-VL-72B, Qwen3-235B) that are given the ground-truth forgery type and artifact taxonomy, i.e., the reasoning is constructed post-hoc from the answer, not derived from perception. Reasoning quality is then judged by GPT-4o/Gemini judges (Table 7), creating a circular LLM-generated/LLM-judged loop. The paper provides no human evaluation of faithfulness, no artifact-grounding metrics, and no way to distinguish genuine evidential reasoning from plausible hallucination.

Potential label/dataset leakage in annotation. Real-image annotation injects dataset-level 'difficulty' labels (Figure 31) derived from dataset identity (e.g., LFW = hard), effectively leaking provenance information into training supervision. Since cross-domain evaluation includes unseen dataset sources, the boundary between learned reasoning and memorized source-distribution cues is unclear.

Metric choices favor the proposed method and obscure failure modes. The main results report only Accuracy; the appendix reveals severe precision/recall asymmetries (e.g., VERITAS reaches 54.7 recall on DeepFaceLab with recall 100 vs. precision 54.7; IC-Light recall drops to 51.5), and no AUC or per-subset error analysis in the main text. Saturated near-99.9% numbers on several cross-model subsets also raise questions about benchmark discriminative power at the high end.

The benchmark's own construction choices may bias results in favor of MLLM-based high-resolution reasoning: low-quality datasets (DFDC, DFDCP, WDF) are explicitly excluded for 'quality control', and the analysis itself notes the model fails on low-resolution data while benefiting from dynamic high-resolution processing. This narrows the claimed 'in-the-wild' coverage.

Fair comparison caveats remain. VERITAS-MINI restricts training scope for MLLM-detector comparison, but the baselines' training data, tuning budgets, and prompts differ in ways that are hard to fully audit; cross-benchmark AIGIBench evaluation also modifies the test set (substituting real images with VFHQ), which weakens comparability with prior reported results.

Writing and presentation issues: an empty 'Project Page:' placeholder and no explicit data/code release commitment undermines reproducibility for what is primarily a benchmark paper; several figures (Figure 2d, 3) are dense and hard to read; minor inconsistencies (appendix lists both A.1.4 Cross-Forgery and A.1.5 Cross-Model headings, missing A.10 in the TOC order).

strengths: Substantial and timely benchmark contribution: HydraFake (100K images) covers classic, public, and self-constructed advanced deepfakes (face restoration, relighting, IP-preserved personalization, VAR-based generation), with a hierarchical four-level evaluation protocol (in-domain, cross-model, cross-forgery, cross-domain) that meaningfully better reflects practical deployment than the standard FF++-training protocol.

Extensive and convincing empirical evaluation: 10 fine-tuned SOTA vision detectors, 6 general MLLMs, and 5 MLLM-based forgery detectors are compared; the paper demonstrates a clear, well-motivated finding that existing detectors generalize on cross-model but fail on cross-forgery/cross-domain splits, and VERITAS achieves ~6% averaged gains with a fair VERITAS-MINI variant for restricted-training comparisons.

Thorough ablation and analysis coverage: reasoning paradigm comparisons (Table 2), training-stage ablations (Fig. 4), reward function ablations (Table 3), pattern-by-pattern removal (Table 5), MiPO non-preference ablations (Table 6), base-model scaling (Table 4), hyperparameters, reward-model choice, P-GRPO data selection, robustness to JPEG/blur, and efficiency analysis collectively support the design choices rather than leaving them as post-hoc justifications.

Strong results relative to much larger closed models: VERITAS (8B) surpasses Gemini-2.5-Pro by 11.8% averaged and generalizes to external benchmarks (LOKI, FakeClue, AIGIBench, Nano-banana) without non-facial training data, supporting the claimed OOD generalization rather than benchmark overfitting.

Transparent methodology for reproducibility: full prompt templates for data annotation, training, reward models, and evaluation are provided; the annotation pipeline (MLLM ensemble voting, artifact taxonomy, multi-step reasoning conversion) is described in detail, and reasoning quality is evaluated with both score-based and pairwise ELO protocols.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: the pipeline combines known ingredients (SFT cold-start, DPO-style preference optimization, GRPO with shaped rewards). The 'pattern-aware' reward and MiPO (mixed rejected traces) are sensible but incremental refinements; the five thinking patterns are heuristic tag-based design choices rather than a principled framework, and their benefit is largely validated only empirically on this dataset.

Potential circularity and bias in training data construction: SFT reasoning traces are generated primarily by MLLMs (Qwen2.5-VL-72B, Qwen3-235B), and reasoning quality is judged by GPT-4o/Gemini-2.5-Pro. This risks annotator bias and favoring stylistic properties that the generator/judge models themselves produce; only ~3K MiPO preference pairs involve human annotation, so the fidelity of the majority of 'human-aligned' reasoning data is not independently verified.

Possible leakage-like effects in evaluation: near-ceiling cross-model accuracy (99.8-99.9% on FLUX/HART/Infinity) for an 8B model trained only on Bearer [REDACTED] raises the question of whether easily detectable generator-specific artifacts (resolution, post-processing cues) dominate these splits; the paper's own results show severe weakness on low-resolution real/fake subsets (e.g., DeepFaceLab 58.6%, FFIW 78.5%), suggesting performance may partly track resolution/quality confounds rather than genuine forgery understanding.

Main-table comparison uses accuracy alone; class imbalance and the demonstrated real-vs-fake precision asymmetries (visible in the appendix) are not reflected in headline claims, which could overstate practical robustness. LLM-as-judge based reasoning-quality metrics also lack human agreement statistics.

Minor reproducibility and presentation issues: the Project Page field is empty; training is described on nonstandard 'PPUE' GPUs without full software details; several baselines (FakeShield, M2F2-Det, SIDA) were not retrained on HydraFake training data, complicating the fairness of the MLLM-detector comparison despite the VERITAS-MINI mitigation.

The claim that pattern-aware reasoning is the key driver would be strengthened by testing on an additional external benchmark within the main ablations; currently, the reasoning-paradigm ablations are confined to HydraFake splits constructed by the authors.
